The core tension arises from AI systems' tendency to assign deterministic labels (e.g., [VERIFIED]) to uncertain or evolving domains such as law and intellectual property. This manifests as a failure mode where confidence is conflated with truth, especially when legal precedents are unsettled. In the case of click-to-cancel, Grok incorrectly labeled a vacated rule as active, violating the NUMBERS LAW and introducing a dangerous misalignment between practice and legal standing. Similarly, nflverse's licensing model was misrepresented due to lack of granular data-source tracking. These errors reflect a deeper issue: the system treats compressed AI outputs as authoritative without sufficient grounding in primary sources. The epistemic structure must distinguish between actionable UX practices and legally binding rules, ensuring that policy decisions are grounded in verifiable facts rather than speculative inference. The mathematical framework requires a calibrated belief update mechanism that penalizes overconfidence in uncertain domains.
